messages.subject: Estimates when using 'scale' in distsamp
messages.subject_clean: Estimates when using 'scale' in distsamp
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question regarding the interpretation of estimates when using the function scale. I used the funcion as follows (inside the distsamp function):

E <- distsamp(~1~scale(Elevation_meters),c,unitsOut = "kmsq")

Are the estimates values the ones I should report? Or are this transformed?  I already predicted densities and I had no problem, but I also want to report the estimates of the model.

Thank you very much for your help!

Best,

Laura

messages.subject: occupancy using categorical predictor with 0 observations category
messages.subject_clean: occupancy using categorical predictor with 0 observations category
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have trouble understanding why unmarked is giving me incorrect results when I use categorical predictors.

I collected data on elephant presence on 3 natural reserves which are managed differently. I am trying to predict elephant occupancy using a multivariate model with function occu(). Most of my variables are continuous except for variables “Reserve management” and “Habitat” that are categorical.

The data shows 0 observations at reserve 1, 40 observations at reserve 2 and 7 observations at reserve 3. You don’t need to be statistician to realize that elephants are almost absent in reserve 1 and 3, however these are the results I get when I use only this variable as predictor:

rsrv=occu(~Camera.type~Nom.Reserve,Eleph)
rsrv

Call:
occu(formula = ~Camera.type ~ Reserve, data = Eleph)

Occupancy:
                  Estimate       SE       z  P(>|z|)
(Intercept)         -1.69    0.335 -5.0408 4.63e-07
Reserve1            -17.46 1398.101 -0.0125 9.90e-01
Reserve3             -1.68    0.657 -2.5543 1.06e-02

Detection:
                     Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)
(Intercept)            -2.418 0.277 -8.73 2.66e-18
Camera.typeCuddeback   -0.686 0.654 -1.05 2.95e-01

AIC: 320.9485

This shows that there is a significant difference between reserve 2 and 3 (p=0.01) (so far so good) but no difference between reserve 2 and 1 (p=0.99) even though reserve 1 has no observations. Also the SE for reserve1 is ridiculously high.

I guess that unmarked doesn’t like categories where observations are 0 or close to 0 but how could I fix this problem knowing that I want to show that there is a difference in occupancy for elephant even when other factors like distance to water or distance to village are controlled?

Thanks a lot in advance!

Gabriel Valdez

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] occupancy using categorical predictor with 0 observations category
messages.body_plain:
Tranquilo, hombre,

unmarked is doing exactly the right thing. The estimate of occupancy in the reserve where no elephants were observed is plogis(-17), which is essentially zero. For such a boundary estimate (i.e., 0 or 1 for a probabillity) you can't estimate the standard error numerically, hence, the huge number which you should not interpret (incl. the p-value).

Best regards --  Marc

names(UPSA_obs.covs) <- c("Date")

UPSA_umf_mod_date_visits135 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=pres_abse, siteCovs=UPSA_site.covs,
                                                 obsCovs=UPSA_obs.covs)   # organize data

Florent

Thank you very much Jeffrey! Very helpful. I have one further question, however.

I am not sure if the way that I predicted the values is actually correct. I did this a while ago, but I am having second thoughts now.

So, first I fitted models as I said before (below the example with the model I used to make predictions):

EH_cuad <- distsamp(~1~scale(Elevation)+I(scale(Elevation)^2)+Habitat,  c, unitsOut = "kmsq")

habConst<-data.frame(Elevation=seq(700,3200,length=2500),Updated_Habitat=factor("Primary",levels=unique(can$Habitat)))

Then I used the function predict:

pHabCost <-predict (EH_cuad,type="state",newdata=habConst,appendData=TRUE)

Then I used this data frame to plot density vs elevation. Should I transformed the predicted values afterwards? Or predicted based on transformed elevation values? I think the estimates of density are reasonable, but I am not sure on how 'predict' deals with transformed covariates (specifically when 'scale' is included within the model fitting function). I would really appreciate some thoughts on this matter.

Best regards,

Laura

messages.body_plain:
Yes. I recall removing those missing values. Sorry, should have mentioned that.  If detection info is missing, there's no point including in the model unless you're trying to predict occupancy or detection prob for that suite of covariates (using the 'predict' method for an unmarked FitOccu), in which case you'll need a proper NA value instead of a period.

Those periods gave me SAS nightmares. 😉

Adam

messages.subject: type argument in unmarkedFrameOccuFP
messages.subject_clean: type argument in unmarkedFrameOccuFP
messages.body_plain:
Hi;
I'm having trouble finding documentation about using the type argument in unmarkedFrameOccuFP. It appears that it is a vector describing the type of data during each occasion in order from left to right in the data matrix (y). So, if I have data of type 1 (certain detection method, no false positives) for the first 3 occasions and then 2 occasions with a method that might have false detections, I would specify type=c(3,2,0). Would someone please verify if this is this correct?

If correct, then for a situation in which the certain detection method followed the uncertain in time, I believe it would be necessary to change the order in the data matrix to have the type 1 occasions followed by type 2 - this might make modeling temporal trends challenging!

Thanks,
Eric

Hi Eric -

You are correct in how to specify data types.

As far as temporal trends, occuFP only deals with single season models (Presence and Mark both have multiseason models implemented now). If the interest is temporal trends in detection, then as you note you can not change the order of the data matrix, and instead need to reorder the covariate that will be used to match the temporal order of visits.

messages.subject: How to deal with clusters in gdistsamp
messages.subject_clean: How to deal with clusters in gdistsamp
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I've collected data to estimate population density and size of a passerine species using a distance sampling protocol. In fact I've run all my analyses in Distance sampling software, but I also collect habitat covariates, so I've decided to model my data using HDS.

 I'm using gdistsamp as I visited all sites 3 times. (numPrimary=3).  In most cases my target species is detected in pairs of birds, but I have detection of up to 4 individuals, and distance data was collected to the center of the cluster, so my question is: Is there a way to deal with clusters in gdistsamp?  I've tried to find discussions about it in the forum and go through the package vignette, but couldn't find anything.

If there is no way to work with clusters in HDS, since I've obtained a mean cluster size in conventional Distance Sampling analysis, would it still be reasonable to run HDS models using detection of clusters to obtain the magnitude of how density varies in relation to certain habitat variables? Instead of modelling distance to individuals, as in this case I'd be violating the independence assumption.

I really appreciate if someone could help me with this.

Best,

Fernanda Alves

messages.body_plain:
Dear Gabriel,

prediction in regression models can be tricky, especialy when there are correlations among the explanatory variables or when not all combinations of covariate values are observed in nature. For instance, it is easy to obtain predictions that do not make sense, even though they are mathematically correct. But the problem is that they may represent an extrapolation into some part of the covariate space that does not exist in practice.

In your model, you predict for the three reserves and keep the values of all the continuous covariates at the mean observed value 0 (assuming that you normalized these covariates). It is easy then that you get predictions for situations that do not exist in practice, because the values of these continuous covariates will NOT be at the observed mean the three reserves. What you do now is predict for a site that lies in each of these three reserves AND has average values of all the continuous covariates in the model. But presumably that combination of covariate values does not exist anywhere in your study area.

If you want to produce a map, then you must supply in your new data frame the values of each covariate for every pixel in the landscape for which you want to predict.

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear Gabriel,

I am a little puzzled, but from looking at your pardus results reported earlier (and somewhere at the bottom of this mail), I get this hunch: I think that in R, the levels of a factor must appear in exactly the same order in the factor that you use to fit the model and in the predict statement. Look at your pardus results again:

> best3=occu(~Camera.type~Dist.Water.Main.Secon_s+Nom.Reserve,Pardus)
> best3

Call:
occu(formula = ~Camera.type ~ Dist.Water.Main.Secon_s + Nom.Reserve,
    data = Pardus)

Occupancy:

(Intercept)               -2.065 0.644 -3.21 0.00134
Dist.Water.Main.Secon_s   -0.883 0.347 -2.54 0.01101
Nom.ReserveM               2.031 0.878  2.31 0.02068
Nom.ReserveR               1.264 0.768  1.64 0.10007

[.....]

> newData=data.frame(Nom.Reserve=c("M","R","RW"),Dist.Water.Main.Secon_s=c(0,0,0))
> pred=predict(best3,type="state",newdata=newData,appendData=T)
> pred

You have different orders of the factor levels. In the fitted model (i.e., in the factor ‘Nom.Reserve’ used to fit the model), the intercept and hence the first (reference) level seems to be RW and then the 2nd and 3rd levels are M and R. In contrast, the ordering of the factor levels in ‘Nom.Reserve’ in the predict command is M, R, RW. It seems that predict produces predictions of the reserved IN THE SAME order as in the fitted model, i.e., first comes RW, then M and finally R. Look at this:

> plogis(-2.065)

[1] 0.1125455

This is essentially identical for the prediction for the first level (RW), which, however, there is erroneously labelled M.

Next, the second prediction is that for the 2nd level IN THE FITTED MODEL (i.e., M)

> plogis(-2.065 + 2.031)

[1] 0.4915008

And, finally, this seems to be the prediction for level R.

> plogis(-2.065 + 1.264)

[1] 0.3098116

Hence, I would try to list the names of the reserves in the Nom.Reserve factor in the predict command in the same order as in the factor used to fit the model and I guess things come out right.

Best regards  --- Marc

Le mardi 18 juillet 2017 18:06:32 UTC+2, Kery Marc a écrit :

Dear Gabriel,

prediction in regression models can be tricky, especialy when there are correlations among the explanatory variables or when not all combinations of covariate values are observed in nature. For instance, it is easy to obtain predictions that do not make sense, even though they are mathematically correct. But the problem is that they may represent an extrapolation into some part of the covariate space that does not exist in practice.

In your model, you predict for the three reserves and keep the values of all the continuous covariates at the mean observed value 0 (assuming that you normalized these covariates). It is easy then that you get predictions for situations that do not exist in practice, because the values of these continuous covariates will NOT be at the observed mean the three reserves. What you do now is predict for a site that lies in each of these three reserves AND has average values of all the continuous covariates in the model. But presumably that combination of covariate values does not exist anywhere in your study area.

If you want to produce a map, then you must supply in your new data frame the values of each covariate for every pixel in the landscape for which you want to predict.

Best regards  --- Marc

> Dear Gabriel,
>
> prediction in regression models can be tricky, especialy when there are correlations among the explanatory variables or when not all combinations of covariate values are observed in nature. For instance, it is easy to obtain predictions that do not make sense, even though they are mathematically correct. But the problem is that they may represent an extrapolation into some part of the covariate space that does not exist in practice.
>
> In your model, you predict for the three reserves and keep the values of all the continuous covariates at the mean observed value 0 (assuming that you normalized these covariates). It is easy then that you get predictions for situations that do not exist in practice, because the values of these continuous covariates will NOT be at the observed mean the three reserves. What you do now is predict for a site that lies in each of these three reserves AND has average values of all the continuous covariates in the model. But presumably that combination of covariate values does not exist anywhere in your study area.
>
> If you want to produce a map, then you must supply in your new data frame the values of each covariate for every pixel in the landscape for which you want to predict.
>
> Best regards  --- Marc

Le mardi 18 juillet 2017 18:06:32 UTC+2, Kery Marc a écrit :

Dear Gabriel,

prediction in regression models can be tricky, especialy when there are correlations among the explanatory variables or when not all combinations of covariate values are observed in nature. For instance, it is easy to obtain predictions that do not make sense, even though they are mathematically correct. But the problem is that they may represent an extrapolation into some part of the covariate space that does not exist in practice.

In your model, you predict for the three reserves and keep the values of all the continuous covariates at the mean observed value 0 (assuming that you normalized these covariates). It is easy then that you get predictions for situations that do not exist in practice, because the values of these continuous covariates will NOT be at the observed mean the three reserves. What you do now is predict for a site that lies in each of these three reserves AND has average values of all the continuous covariates in the model. But presumably that combination of covariate values does not exist anywhere in your study area.

If you want to produce a map, then you must supply in your new data frame the values of each covariate for every pixel in the landscape for which you want to predict.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
It worked!!!!!! Thanks a million times!

What i needed to do was to relevel the newData$Nom.Reserve just as i did in the original data before doing the prediction.

newData$Nom.Reserve=relevel(newData$Nom.Reserve,ref="Rukwa")

Marc was right, it was the right prediction but in the wrong order.

I've being struggling with these weird results for days.

You both are my heros, thank you very much.

messages.body_plain:
I just wanted to follow up on your comment "Turns out I am not supposed to interpret parameters with huge SE."  That's an incorrect interpretation of what Marc Kery told you.  He told you exactly what what the issue is.

The maximum likelihood estimator for that probability is 0 (which translates to minus infinity in the logit scale) and is on the border of the parameter space.  (Same thing when the probability is estimated to be 1).  In such cases one cannot (using maximum likelihood) estimate the associated estimate of precision.  That's just a fact of life with maximum likelihood estimation.

Because unmarked uses iterative methods to find the maximum likelihood estimates, the estimation procedure stops when the function being optimized stops changing by a preset amount.  (It's a little more complicated than that but close.)  For your data it stopped when the estimate for ReserveM was -17.46 which (as Marc pointed out) corresponds essentially to a probability of zero just as it would be if minus infinity was given as the estimate on the logit scale.

So (to finally make the point) it is the parameter estimate being very negative is what is important and not the size of the reported standard error.

OK.  End of sermon.

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I get the feeling this is probably pretty easy and straight forward.  But, I’m new to unmarked, and fairly new to R as well.  I’m analysing occupancy (occupancy and detection probability) for introduced rats on islands in an archipelago in the tropical Pacific using ‘occu’.  I have two replicates of 100 samples each, collected at 50 sample stations on tourist visited islands and 50 on non-tourist visited islands.  My covariate (‘siteCovs’) is thus “tourist”.  All went smoothly until I tried to backTransform occupancy (‘state’ variable) in my model with the covariate (as I’d read would happen).  However, I’m not entirely sure how to use the linearComb feature to produce as “scalar linear combination” that I can then backTransform.  Here is what it looks like (please forgive the sloppiness - I copied and pasted from history in R Studio):

Call:
occu(formula = ~1 ~ Tourist, data = umf)

Occupancy:
            Estimate     SE     z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)    0.984  0.344 2.863 0.00419
Tourist        9.640 41.505 0.232 0.81633

Detection:
 Estimate    SE    z  P(>|z|)
     1.41 0.207 6.85 7.56e-12

AIC: 226.0303
> backTransform(fm2['det'])
Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Detection estimate(s)

 Estimate     SE LinComb (Intercept)
    0.804 0.0325    1.41           1

Transformation: logistic
> backTransform(fm2['state'])
Error in .local(obj, ...) :
  Cannot directly back-transform an unmarkedEstimate with length > 1.
Use linearComb() and then backTransform() the resulting scalar linear combination.

I tried to take a stab at this, based on material I had read and seen online, but I'm not sure this is correct:

> lcfm2 <- linearComb(fm2, c(1,1), type='state')
> lcfm2
Linear combination(s) of Occupancy estimate(s)

 Estimate   SE (Intercept) Tourist
     10.6 41.5           1       1

> backTransform(lcfm2)
Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Occupancy estimate(s)

 Estimate      SE LinComb (Intercept) Tourist
        1 0.00101    10.6           1       1

Transformation: logistic

Am I close???  Thanks for any and all help, and your patience...

Paul Radley

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

I think I would ALWAYS just use the predict function for prediction. In your case, do something analogous to the following (hab is a factor with three levels):

# Fit model p(time+wind), psi(hab)

summary(fm2.occ <- occu(~time+wind-1 ~hab, data=umf))

# Predict occupancy for habitat factor levels

newdat <- data.frame(hab = c("A", "B", "C"))

predict(fm2.occ, type="state", newdata = newdat, appendData = TRUE)

This gives this:
  Predicted         SE      lower     upper hab
1 0.1139666 0.07914607 0.02693418 0.3741059   A
2 0.6579139 0.15598369 0.33084338 0.8820925   B
3 0.7100853 0.13388848 0.40639000 0.8975695   C

Which is what you want.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Paul,

couple of things.

First, with only a single visit, one cannot separately estimate occupancy and detection probability. This explains the strange result (you see twice the same numbers). You must ignore this. (When you have continuous covariates, and some affect exclusively occupancy and the other(s) exclusively detection, you can separately estimate both components of the model, but such an analysis may not be very robust and care has to be taken).

Second, you have count data and hence much more information about the local populations than just presence/absence. I would convert counts to detection/nondetection data only very exceptionally, since you throw out information. In your case, I would fit a Poisson regression, knowing and acknowledging openly that the modelled quantity is not the expected abundance, but the expectation of the product of abundance and detection at each site. This is what 80-90% of all people in Ecology do, so it is unlikely that you will be slayed. Think hard about possible covariates that could act on detection and that, in your case, will show up on the expectation of abundance and detection: they can feign a relationship with abundance that's not there, make it weaker or stronger or mask it. Discuss this.

For single-visit count data, there is also the possibility to separate detection and abundance with continuous covariates,  but I would not recommend such an analysis, because it is extremely dependent on the parametric assumptions of the model, see  http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12507/abstract and also  http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12329/abstract and (for an opposing view)  http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/env.1149/full

Third, there is more to these methods (occupancy, Nmix models) than just running a canned function in R. It would be good it you could read up on them to improve your understanding of the basics.

Best regards  --  Marc

messages.subject_clean: pcountOpen : problem when adding covariates for abundance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Clemence,

For dynamic models like the Dail-Madsen (pcountopen) or dynamic occupancy models (colext), the site-specific state variable (N, in this case) can initially be modeled (primary occasion 1) as a function of covariates, but is subsequently a function of the parameters describing the dynamics...in your case, with the 'trend'  formulation:

N[i,1]~Poisson(lambda[i])
N[i, 2]~Poisson(N[i, 1] * gamma[i, 1]). [Or maybe some alternative distribution].

Because of the way the model likelihood is set up, you can't directly model variability in N as related to covariates each year; instead, you can model variability in gamma for each primary period*site after the first period. One workaround is to "stack the data" and fit a standard Nmix model (pcount) to each primary period *site combination. I think the first example of doing so is here (using BUGS):

Kery, M., Dorazio, R., Soldaat, L., Van Strien, A., Zuiderwijk, A., and Royle, J. (2009), “Trend estimation in populations with imperfect detection,” Journal of Applied Ecology, 46, 1163–1172.

If you search for "stack or stacking data" on the list, you should find plenty of further descriptions applicable to analysis in unmarked.

Cheers,

John

messages.subject: Unusually low detection probability obtained from pcount data?
messages.subject_clean: Unusually low detection probability obtained from pcount data?
messages.body_plain:
My name is Chris, a biologist just learning to use unmarked.  I have 3 replicated visits to 19 point count locations, in this case for Bairds Trogon in Costa Rica.  The data looks like this:
     X Occasion1 Occasion2 Occasion3
1  N01         1         0         0
2  N02         0         2         0
3  N03         1         1         0
4  N04         0         0         0
5  N05         0         1         0
6  N06         0         0         0
7  N07         1         1         0
8  N08         0         1         0
9  N09         0         1         1
10 S01         1         1         1
11 S02         0         0         1
12 S03         0         0         0
13 S04         1         1         0
14 S05         0         0         0
15 S06         0         0         1
16 S07         2         0         0
17 S08         0         1         0
18 S09         1         0         0
19 S10         0         0         0

batrog.frame <- unmarkedFramePcount(y=batrog.y)
 mNull <- pcount(~1 ~1,, data= batrog.frame)
backTransform(mNull, type="det")
Backtransformed linear combination(s) of Detection estimate(s)

 Estimate      SE LinComb (Intercept)
  0.00573 0.00635   -5.16
  1
I ran a model with pcount function, using an intercept only model for both state and detection.  It is estimating 67 trogons per point (which have 100 m radius), with a detection probability of .005!  I have worked through every example I can find online and can't find any mistakes in my short bit of code. My mentors all say this detection probability is way too low for this sort of data, and my density should be around 1-5 birds max.  Any ideas what I am doing wrong? Thanks!

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Unusually low detection probability obtained from pcount data?
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Unusually low detection probability obtained from pcount data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

In my opinion, to fit a N-mix with your data need more sites and/or use covariates. If you try to “reduce” your data (something like y[y>1]<-1) to make an occupancy model, you will obtain a high occupancy and a realistic detection probability of 0.351 (SE:0.0644).

Best,

Jose

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Estimate c-hat via AICcmodavg for pcount model
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Estimate c-hat via AICcmodavg for pcount model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bill,

c_hat( ) is to compute the c-hat for classic Poisson or binomial GLM's. If you want to assess model fit with pcount models, you should be using Nmix.gof.test( ). See ?Nmix.gof.test for an example.

Best,

Marc

Objet : [unmarked] Estimate c-hat via AICcmodavg for pcount model

Hello,

This is kind of a cross-over question between Unmarked and AICcmodavg packages.  I am attempting to estimate the potential for overdispersion for my global count model.

Here is my code for the global model:

(eubiAfm22 <- pcount(~survey + I(julian_std^2) + julian_std + year + ecoregion ~I(cond_score_std^2) + cond_score_std, eubiA.umf)) #eubi global model

Model runs fine, but when I try to estimate c-hat based on recommendations in AICcmodavg as follows:

c_hat(eubiAfm22)

I get this message:

Error in c_hat.default(eubiAfm1) :
Function not yet defined for this object class

My understanding was that c_hat was appropriated for N-mixture models and Poisson count models.

Thanks for any help.

Bill Sutton

--
